alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

anticholinergic-toxicity.name: Anticholinergic toxicity
anticholinergic-toxicity.scope: Antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, atropine, anticholinergic toxidrome, physostigmine
anticholinergic-toxicity.core: Delirium with mydriasis, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention, and reduced bowel sounds after muscarinic blockade.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diphenhydramine, other first-generation antihistamines, atropine, scopolamine, tricyclic antidepressants, toxic plants
Older age, polypharmacy, accidental pediatric ingestion, intentional overdose; mixed toxidromes are common

rows.label: Clues
items: Agitation, hallucinations, picking at unseen objects, blurred vision, tachycardia
★ **Hot and dry**, rather than sweaty; severe poisoning causes seizures, coma, dysrhythmias
Palpable bladder, ileus; TCA exposure may add hypotension and conduction abnormalities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central/peripheral muscarinic antagonism; some causative drugs also block sodium channels
Absent sweating impairs heat dissipation; agitation further increases temperature

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome + ECG**; check QRS/QTc before considering reversal
Glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, CK; acetaminophen level for uncertain intentional ingestion
TCA markers: QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR signals sodium-channel toxicity
Drug screens do not establish severity; ECG and physiology drive treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, IV fluids, external cooling; **benzodiazepines** for agitation/seizures
Bladder catheter for retention; activated charcoal early only with protected airway and toxicology advice
★ Pure severe antimuscarinic delirium → selected **physostigmine**, slow IV with continuous monitoring and expert supervision
Avoid physostigmine with suspected TCA/mixed cardiotoxic ingestion, QRS widening, significant conduction disease, or seizures
Sodium-channel blockade → **IV sodium bicarbonate**; avoid QT-prolonging antipsychotics in high-risk poisoning

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, aspiration, heat injury, ventricular arrhythmia, death
Physostigmine → bradycardia, seizures, asystole in unsuitable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce anticholinergic burden, safe storage, avoid duplicate OTC sleep/cold products; assess intent after stabilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sympathomimetic toxicity: diaphoresis and active bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, dopamine-blocker exposure

bell-palsy.name: Bell palsy
bell-palsy.scope: Idiopathic facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, forehead involvement vs central sparing, eye care, oral glucocorticoids, Lyme disease facial palsy
bell-palsy.core: Acute unilateral peripheral facial weakness includes the forehead; protect the cornea and treat early after excluding secondary causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/postpartum period, diabetes; often follows viral illness
Tick exposure/endemic region suggests Lyme; otalgia with vesicles suggests varicella-zoster

rows.label: Clues

items: Inflammation and edema of CN VII within facial canal impair ipsilateral facial muscles

★ **Artificial tears**, nighttime eye ointment and taping; urgent ophthalmology for corneal injury

Ramsay Hunt syndrome → valacyclovir plus glucocorticoid; antivirals alone insufficient for idiopathic palsy

carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease
chronic-kidney-disease.scope: CKD progression, anemia of CKD (erythropoietin deficiency), mineral and bone disorder, uremic complications, volume overload, indications for emergent dialysis (AEIOU), vascular access
chronic-kidney-disease.core: Persistent kidney injury or reduced filtration causes progressive cardiovascular, metabolic and uremic complications; dialysis follows clinical indications rather than creatinine alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease, obstruction, recurrent AKI, inherited cystic disease
NSAIDs, smoking and uncontrolled proteinuria accelerate progression

rows.label: Clues
items: Early disease often asymptomatic; advanced disease → fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, edema
Uremia: confusion, pericardial friction rub, nausea or bleeding despite normal platelet count
Labs: normocytic anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, ↑phosphate, low/normal calcium

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nephron loss → hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, proteinuria and fibrosis
↓Erythropoietin causes anemia; phosphate retention/↓calcitriol → secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **eGFR <60** or kidney-damage markers for **≥3 months** establishes CKD
Urine albumin/creatinine ratio, urinalysis, creatinine trend; ultrasound for size/obstruction
Stage by GFR and albuminuria; small echogenic kidneys support chronicity but are not universal
Monitor CBC, ferritin/TSAT, K, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and PTH

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Albuminuric CKD → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**; monitor creatinine/K; never combine both
SGLT2 inhibitor for T2DM or qualifying albuminuric CKD/HF, generally starting eGFR ≥20
Overload → salt restriction, furosemide; high phosphate → sevelamer; selected severe hyperparathyroidism → calcitriol
Iron repletion before ESA for selected persistent anemia; correct clinically significant metabolic acidosis
★ **Dialysis (AEIOU)**: refractory acidosis/hyperkalemia/overload, dialyzable toxins, uremic complications

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiovascular death, fractures, severe hyperkalemic arrhythmia, malnutrition
Dialysis access infection/thrombosis; rapid urea reduction → dialysis disequilibrium

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Preserve arm veins; plan **AV fistula** before hemodialysis; temporary catheter for emergencies; early transplant referral
BP/glycemic control, avoid nephrotoxins, renal drug adjustment; hepatitis B vaccination before dialysis

rows.label: Mimics
items: AKI: acute creatinine change; may complicate established CKD
Prerenal azotemia: reversible perfusion deficit without persistent structural injury

cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.name: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.scope: Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, esophageal varices, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma screening
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.core: Cirrhosis produces portal hypertension and synthetic failure; new ascites, bleeding, confusion or kidney injury signals decompensation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol, chronic HBV/HCV, metabolic steatotic liver disease; autoimmune/cholestatic disorders

rows.label: Clues
items: Splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas, jaundice, muscle wasting
Encephalopathy triggers: GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, hypokalemia
SBP may present only with subtle confusion or renal deterioration; fever/pain can be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fibrosis raises intrahepatic resistance; splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume
Portal collaterals bleed; impaired toxin clearance causes neuropsychiatric dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New/worsening or hospitalized ascites → **diagnostic paracentesis**; PMN **≥250/µL** → treat SBP
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension; send ascitic culture in bedside blood-culture bottles
HRS-AKI: exclude shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction and structural injury; assess volume response
MELD-Na/MELD 3.0 guides prognosis/transplant assessment; ammonia does not establish encephalopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Variceal bleed → resuscitate, **octreotide + ceftriaxone**, urgent endoscopic banding; refractory → TIPS
Ascites → sodium restriction, spironolactone ± furosemide; tense ascites → paracentesis, albumin if >5 L
★ SBP → **ceftriaxone**, albumin for high-risk renal/liver dysfunction; reassess response
Encephalopathy → lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day; recurrent episodes → add rifaximin; correct trigger
HRS → stop diuretics/nephrotoxins, **terlipressin + albumin** after volume assessment; monitor hypoxia; transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: HCC, recurrent infection, malnutrition, hepatopulmonary syndrome; TIPS can worsen encephalopathy
Avoid NSAIDs, sedatives and unnecessary fluid loading; INR alone poorly predicts procedural bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months** for HCC surveillance in eligible cirrhosis
Carvedilol for clinically significant portal hypertension when tolerated; banding if indicated and beta blocker unsuitable
After SBP → antibiotic prophylaxis; alcohol abstinence, hepatitis vaccines, adequate protein intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiac ascites: high SAAG with ascitic protein ≥2.5 g/dL
Malignant/TB ascites: usually low SAAG

congenital-infections.name: Congenital infections
congenital-infections.scope: Cytomegalovirus (sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications), Toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis), Parvovirus B19 (hydrops), Rubella, Varicella, Zika, screening and diagnosis
congenital-infections.core: Congenital infection causes growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, or hydrops; organ-specific patterns identify the pathogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CMV: toddler saliva/urine; toxoplasma: undercooked meat, cat feces; B19: child with slapped-cheek rash
Absent rubella/varicella immunity; mosquito exposure or sexual transmission in Zika-risk areas

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae/blueberry-muffin lesions, abnormal fetal ultrasound; many infected newborns initially appear well
★ B19 hydrops: cardiomegaly, ascites, edema without red-cell alloantibodies

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transplacental infection disrupts organogenesis; later exposure may cause inflammation or marrow suppression
Toxoplasma transmission increases with gestational age; earlier infection causes more severe injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal exposure → pathogen-specific **IgG/IgM**, paired titers or avidity; isolated IgM needs confirmation
★ CMV newborn diagnosis: saliva PCR then confirm urine PCR **within 21 days**
Suspected fetal infection → targeted ultrasound, pathogen-specific amniotic-fluid PCR; B19 → serial MCA Doppler
Prenatal rubella IgG routinely; no universal US maternal CMV, toxoplasma, or B19 screening

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic congenital CMV → **valganciclovir**, monitor CBC and liver tests
Congenital toxoplasmosis → pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin; maternal regimen depends on fetal infection
B19 severe fetal anemia → intrauterine transfusion; rubella/Zika structural injury → supportive care
Maternal varicella exposure without immunity → varicella-zoster immune globulin; maternal pneumonia → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Stillbirth, neurodevelopmental disability; delayed/progressive hearing loss requires longitudinal audiology

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Rubella/varicella vaccination before pregnancy or postpartum; **live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy**
Handwashing after diapers; cook meat, avoid litter handling; mosquito precautions and Zika exposure counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aneuploidy: abnormal genetic testing rather than pathogen testing
Rh disease: positive maternal antibody screen with fetal anemia

table.title: Discriminating congenital patterns
rows: Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss
Severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications, ocular abnormalities

congenital-infections.evidence: CMV testing checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/cytomegalovirus/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); remaining pathogen patterns established teaching.

cranial-nerve-palsies.name: Cranial nerve palsies
cranial-nerve-palsies.scope: CN III palsy, CN IV palsy, CN VI palsy, Bell palsy (CN VII, hyperacusis, corticosteroids), microvascular diabetic neuropathy, cavernous sinus thrombosis
cranial-nerve-palsies.core: Localize diplopia by the weak extraocular muscle; distinguish peripheral facial paralysis from a central lesion by forehead involvement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension → ischemic mononeuropathy; trauma → trochlear injury
Sinusitis or facial infection → cavernous sinus thrombosis; pregnancy associated with Bell palsy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Multiple ocular palsies + fever, proptosis, chemosis** → cavernous sinus thrombosis
Bell palsy: unilateral upper/lower facial weakness, altered taste, hyperacusis; no other focal deficits
Raised ICP may produce unilateral or bilateral abducens palsy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Diabetic ischemia often spares superficial parasympathetic CN III fibers; compression threatens pupil function
CN VII inflammation within facial canal disrupts facial movement and stapedius innervation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute CN III palsy → urgent **CTA/MRA**, especially painful or pupil-involving; exclude aneurysm
Typical isolated Bell palsy: clinical; atypical/recurrent palsy → MRI, targeted Lyme testing
Suspected cavernous thrombosis → contrast MRI/MRV or CT venography; blood cultures

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bell palsy within 72 hours → **prednisone**; add valacyclovir for severe paralysis
★ Artificial tears, nighttime ointment and eyelid taping to protect exposed cornea
Cavernous thrombosis: IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole; source drainage, consider anticoagulation
Microvascular palsy: vascular risk control, temporary patch/prism; reassess if persistent or progressive

rows.label: Complications
items: Exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration; facial synkinesis after recovery
Septic thrombosis → meningitis, stroke, blindness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat facial/sinus infections; optimize diabetes and BP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stroke: forehead relatively spared with contralateral limb findings
Myasthenia: fatigable variable weakness, normal pupils
Ramsay Hunt: ear vesicles and otalgia with facial paralysis

table.title: Ocular localization
rows: Worse downstairs; compensatory opposite head tilt

cranial-nerve-palsies.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-ophthalmology and Bell palsy teaching.

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Disorganized thinking, sleep–wake reversal, hallucinations; hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed presentation
★ Hypoactive withdrawal/lethargy easily missed; **test attention**, not orientation alone
Digit span, months backward or inability to sustain conversation reveals attentional deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance
Multiple small precipitating factors can exceed low cognitive reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline
CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function; targeted cultures, ECG or imaging guided by findings
CT head for focal deficit, trauma or unexplained reduced consciousness; LP for suspected CNS infection
Do not attribute delirium to bacteriuria alone without urinary/systemic infection evidence

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep
Calm environment and familiar support; remove unnecessary catheters and avoid physical restraints
★ Severe distress or danger despite de-escalation → short course **haloperidol**, check QT/EPS risk
Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia → avoid potent dopamine blockers; specialist-guided alternative
Benzodiazepines generally worsen delirium; reserve for withdrawal or selected seizures/catatonia

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, persistent cognitive impairment and increased mortality
Antipsychotics may prolong QT; sedation may conceal clinical deterioration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Multicomponent prevention: orientation, daytime activity, sleep protection, hydration, pain control and drug review
Minimize nighttime interruptions and unnecessary sedatives; encourage family engagement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: chronic progression; attention relatively preserved early
Depression: sustained mood symptoms without fluctuating consciousness
Primary psychosis: usually preserved attention and alertness

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; depression may present as somatic complaints

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, stress responses, and neuroplasticity
Antidepressant benefit develops over weeks despite early changes in neurotransmitter availability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
PHQ-9 quantifies severity; interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **continuous observation and psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe: SSRI such as sertraline + psychotherapy
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid eating disorders; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation, useful with anorexia/insomnia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after starting/changing drugs, family support with consent
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; depressive cognitive impairment often prominent complaints and variable effort
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

diabetic-retinopathy.name: Diabetic retinopathy
diabetic-retinopathy.scope: Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, macular edema, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, neovascularization, panretinal photocoagulation, anti-VEGF
diabetic-retinopathy.core: Diabetes damages retinal microvessels; vision loss comes from macular leakage or ischemia-driven fragile new vessels.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Longer diabetes duration, poor glycemic control, hypertension, nephropathy, dyslipidemia
Pregnancy with preexisting diabetes; rapid glycemic improvement can transiently worsen existing disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic initially; blurred central vision suggests macular involvement
New floaters, haze, sudden painless visual decline suggest vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pericyte loss and basement membrane changes → capillary leakage/closure
Retinal hypoxia → VEGF release; new vessels bleed and contract with fibrous tissue

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Dilated retinal examination**; validated retinal photography programs require timely ophthalmology referral pathways
★ **OCT** quantifies macular edema; fluorescein angiography evaluates leakage/nonperfusion when needed
Prompt ophthalmology referral for any macular edema, moderate-or-worse NPDR, or proliferative disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Optimize **glycemia, BP and lipids** across stages; gradual individualized glucose targets
★ Center-involving edema with impaired acuity → intravitreal **anti-VEGF** such as ranibizumab/aflibercept
High-risk proliferative disease → panretinal photocoagulation; anti-VEGF alternative with reliable follow-up
Persistent vitreous hemorrhage or macula-threatening tractional detachment → vitrectomy
Aspirin for cardiovascular indications remains acceptable; retinopathy alone is not a contraindication

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, neovascular glaucoma; laser may reduce peripheral/night vision
Intravitreal injection: rare endophthalmitis; missed anti-VEGF visits can permit rapid progression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Type 2: screen at diagnosis; type 1: within 5 years after onset; generally repeat annually
No retinopathy and controlled glycemia → consider every 1–2 years; established disease → at least annually
Preexisting diabetes: examination before pregnancy/first trimester and follow-up through pregnancy/postpartum

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypertensive retinopathy: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking; can coexist
Retinal vein occlusion: unilateral sectoral or diffuse venous congestion

table.title: Fundus stages
rows: Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, exudates
Retinal thickening/fluid; possible at any stage

encephalitis.name: Encephalitis
encephalitis.scope: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), temporal lobe lesions, CSF analysis (elevated RBCs, lymphocytic pleocytosis, PCR), IV acyclovir, West Nile virus, autoimmune encephalitis
encephalitis.core: Fever with sustained altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits suggests brain inflammation and warrants immediate empiric acyclovir.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HSV-1 often occurs without immunosuppression; mosquito exposure suggests arboviruses
Autoimmune disease or tumor association; anti-NMDA receptor disease sometimes accompanies ovarian teratoma

rows.label: Clues
items: HSV: personality change, aphasia, olfactory hallucinations, focal seizures
★ **Temporal lobe abnormalities** strongly suggest HSV; hemorrhagic CSF possible but not required
West Nile: movement disorder or asymmetric flaccid weakness; anti-NMDA: psychosis, dyskinesia, autonomic instability
Reduced consciousness, status epilepticus, or respiratory compromise → ICU-level care

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV causes necrotizing inflammation, often limbic/temporal; mosquito-borne viruses infect neuronal tissue
Autoantibodies against neuronal surface antigens disrupt synaptic signaling

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **LP: CSF cells, protein, glucose, HSV PCR**; lymphocytes, ↑protein, usually normal glucose
Neuroimaging before LP for focal deficits, papilledema, marked impaired consciousness, or suspected mass effect
MRI more sensitive than CT; EEG identifies nonconvulsive seizures or temporal periodic discharges
Early negative PCR with strong suspicion → continue treatment and repeat CSF PCR in 3–7 days
West Nile: CSF IgM; autoimmune suspicion → CSF/serum antibodies and tumor search

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected HSV → **IV acyclovir immediately**, usually 14–21 days; do not await PCR
Airway/seizure support; possible bacterial infection → ceftriaxone + vancomycin; Listeria risk → add ampicillin
Acyclovir: renal adjustment, IV hydration; West Nile: supportive care
★ Autoimmune disease → **steroids, IVIG/plasma exchange**, tumor removal after infectious evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, focal deficits, death; acyclovir crystal nephropathy
Severe autoimmune disease: arrhythmia, hypoventilation, prolonged rehabilitation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mosquito repellent, protective clothing, vector control; no routine HSV encephalitis vaccine

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bacterial meningitis: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose; overlap requires empiric coverage
Toxic/metabolic delirium: systemic explanation without inflammatory CSF
Primary psychosis: lacks new seizures, dysautonomia, or focal neurologic abnormalities

encephalitis.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious and autoimmune neurology teaching.

giant-cell-arteritis.name: Giant cell arteritis
giant-cell-arteritis.scope: Giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, vision loss
giant-cell-arteritis.core: New headache with jaw claudication or visual symptoms after age 50 requires immediate glucocorticoids to prevent irreversible blindness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, female sex, Northern European ancestry; frequently overlaps polymyalgia rheumatica
Age <50 makes this diagnosis very unlikely

rows.label: Clues
items: Scalp tenderness, abnormal temporal artery, fever, weight loss, fatigue
★ **Transient monocular loss, diplopia, or sudden painless visual loss** → ocular ischemia
PMR: bilateral shoulder/hip aching, morning stiffness >45 minutes; true muscle strength preserved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Granulomatous inflammation of large/medium arteries → intimal proliferation and ischemic narrowing
Posterior ciliary artery involvement causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ESR/CRP and CBC**: inflammation, thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia support; normal markers do not fully exclude
★ **Temporal artery biopsy** confirms; skip lesions can cause false negative, so obtain adequate segment
Ultrasound halo sign useful in experienced centers; arrange testing promptly after treatment begins
Assess pulses, arm pressures, bruits; CTA/MRA for suspected aortic/branch-vessel involvement
PMR: elevated inflammatory markers, normal CK; screen all PMR patients for cranial/visual symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected cranial GCA → **high-dose oral prednisone now**, before biopsy
★ Threatened or established visual loss → **IV methylprednisolone** urgently; ophthalmology consultation
Taper slowly with symptom/marker monitoring; tocilizumab can reduce steroid exposure in selected patients
Isolated PMR → lower-dose prednisone; failure to improve promptly → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent blindness, often sequential fellow-eye involvement; stroke, aortic aneurysm/dissection
Prolonged steroids → infection, diabetes, cataracts, osteoporosis; IL-6 blockade can suppress inflammatory markers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Bone protection and fracture-risk assessment during prolonged steroids; monitor BP/glucose
Educate about recurrent visual symptoms, jaw pain, limb claudication; evaluate aorta over time

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy: vascular risks, no systemic inflammatory syndrome
Myositis: objective proximal weakness, elevated CK
TMJ disease: local joint pain/clicking rather than chewing-induced ischemic fatigue

giant-cell-arteritis.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatologic emergency and PMR management.

glycogen-storage-diseases.name: Glycogen storage diseases
glycogen-storage-diseases.scope: Von Gierke disease (type I), Pompe disease (type II), Cori disease (type III), McArdle disease (type V), exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria, fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly
glycogen-storage-diseases.core: Inherited glycogen disorders separate into fasting-intolerant hepatic disease, exercise-intolerant skeletal muscle disease, and infantile cardiomyopathy with hypotonia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually autosomal recessive; consanguinity or affected siblings; presentation from infancy to adulthood

rows.label: Clues
items: Hepatic forms: hepatomegaly and fasting intolerance; hypoglycemic seizures possible
★ **Second-wind phenomenon** after brief rest or reduced intensity suggests muscle phosphorylase deficiency
★ Floppy infant with **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**, macroglossia and respiratory weakness → urgent metabolic evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective glycogen synthesis/breakdown impairs glucose release or muscle energy supply
Lysosomal glycogen accumulation uniquely produces the multisystem storage phenotype in type II

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, lactate, lipids, uric acid, CK**, liver enzymes; correlate abnormalities with phenotype
Enzyme assay and molecular testing confirm subtype; echocardiography when cardiac involvement possible
Suspected muscle glycogenosis: exercise-associated CK/myoglobin elevation; nonischemic forearm testing may support diagnosis
Avoid diagnostic prolonged fasting in infants or severe hypoglycemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hepatic forms: **frequent feeds/uncooked cornstarch**; acute hypoglycemia or no enteral intake → IV dextrose
Type I: restrict fructose/galactose; monitor metabolic control and renal/hepatic disease
Type III: high-protein diet plus fasting avoidance; individualized cornstarch
Type II: **alglucosidase alfa** enzyme replacement promptly; ventilatory/cardiac support
Type V: graded aerobic conditioning, avoid intense isometric exertion; simple carbohydrate before planned exercise

rows.label: Complications
items: Type I: hepatic adenomas, CKD, gout; type III: fibrosis and cardiomyopathy
Muscle forms: rhabdomyolysis, AKI; untreated infantile type II: cardiorespiratory failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Genetic counseling; sick-day feeding plans and avoidance of prolonged fasting in hepatic disease
Educate muscle-disease patients to stop exertion for cramps/dark urine and maintain hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Fatty-acid oxidation defects: fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia, abnormal acylcarnitines
Muscular dystrophy: progressive weakness rather than episodic metabolic exercise intolerance

table.title: Enzyme and pattern
rows: Exercise cramps/myoglobinuria; flat exercise lactate rise

glycogen-storage-diseases.evidence: Not checked online; established metabolic phenotypes and foundational management.

hearing-loss.name: Hearing loss
hearing-loss.scope: Conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss, Weber and Rinne tests, presbycusis, ototoxicity (cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics), noise-induced, Meniere disease, acoustic neuroma
hearing-loss.core: Distinguish impaired sound conduction from cochlear/nerve dysfunction; sudden sensorineural loss requires urgent treatment rather than observation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Aging, occupational/recreational noise, cerumen, chronic middle-ear disease
★ Ototoxins: **cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics**; risk increases with renal impairment and combined exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency loss, difficulty understanding speech amid background noise
Noise injury: high-frequency audiometric notch; tinnitus common
Ménière: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
★ **Unilateral progressive loss + poor speech discrimination** → vestibular schwannoma; imbalance may accompany

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conductive: external/middle-ear transmission impaired; sensorineural: cochlea or auditory nerve damaged
Chronic noise/aging preferentially damages basal cochlear hair cells; Ménière involves endolymphatic hydrops

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy → tuning forks → formal audiometry**, including air/bone thresholds and speech testing
Tympanometry evaluates middle-ear mechanics; asymmetric sensorineural loss → MRI internal auditory canals
Sudden loss: ≥30 dB across ≥3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours; urgent audiogram/ENT
Do not attribute sudden unilateral deficit to cerumen without confirming resolution after removal

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove cerumen, treat effusion/infection or structural cause; persistent conductive disease → ENT
★ Sudden sensorineural loss → **corticosteroids promptly**, within 2 weeks; intratympanic route possible
Chronic bilateral deficit → hearing aids, communication strategies; severe refractory loss → cochlear implant evaluation
Ménière: sodium moderation, selected diuretic; short-term vestibular suppressant during attacks
Vestibular schwannoma: observation, stereotactic radiation, or surgery according to tumor size and symptoms

rows.label: Complications
items: Communication barriers, social isolation, depression, impaired safety awareness
Ototoxicity can be permanent; vestibular injury can cause imbalance and falls

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hearing protection, safe listening levels, baseline/serial audiometry with ototoxic drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Auditory processing/cognitive disorder: difficulty understanding despite relatively preserved peripheral thresholds
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without hearing loss

herpes-zoster.name: Herpes zoster
herpes-zoster.scope: Varicella zoster reactivation, dermatomal rash, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, oral antivirals, postherpetic neuralgia, Shingrix vaccine
herpes-zoster.core: Latent varicella-zoster reactivation causes painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles; ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease changes urgency and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, HIV, malignancy, transplantation, immunosuppressive drugs
Previous chickenpox or live varicella vaccination establishes latency; no new exposure required

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning/allodynia can precede eruption by days; crops crust over approximately 7–10 days
★ **V1 distribution, nasal-tip lesions, eye pain** → urgent ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus
★ **Ear vesicles + ipsilateral facial paralysis** ± hearing/vestibular symptoms → Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Multiple noncontiguous dermatomes or >20 lesions outside primary/adjacent dermatomes suggests dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced VZV-specific cellular immunity permits virus to travel from sensory ganglion to skin
Neuronal inflammation/injury explains acute pain and persistent neuropathic symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical eruption → **clinical diagnosis**; atypical lesions → vesicle-base VZV PCR
Assess ocular, neurologic, and systemic findings; consider immunodeficiency evaluation for unusually severe/recurrent disease
CSF PCR for suspected CNS infection; do not delay treatment in high-risk presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir** ideally within 72 hours; still treat new lesions or complications
Dissemination, visceral/CNS disease, severe immunosuppression → **IV acyclovir**
Acute pain: acetaminophen/NSAID, add neuropathic agent when needed; avoid routine systemic steroids
Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus glucocorticoid early; eye lubrication/protection for incomplete closure
Postherpetic neuralgia: gabapentin/pregabalin, topical lidocaine, selected TCA; no antiviral benefit after resolved eruption

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent pain >90 days, secondary bacterial infection, corneal injury, vision loss
Meningoencephalitis, vasculopathy, visceral spread in vulnerable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Shingrix two doses** for adults ≥50 years or immunocompromised ≥19 years, including prior zoster
Cover lesions until crusted; exposure causes chickenpox in susceptible contacts, not immediate shingles
Disseminated: airborne/contact until crusted; immunocompromised localized: same precautions until dissemination excluded

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: recurrent localized lesions, often oral/genital rather than a full dermatome
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure pattern, no neuropathic prodrome

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection: fever, rash, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy after recent exposure
Weight loss, oral thrush, recurrent infections suggest advanced immunodeficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB testing; pregnancy assessment
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin or TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary brain lesion, fails empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; induced sputum/BAL

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine; postoperative pain, nausea, endurance exercise
Pulmonary/CNS disease, malignancy; heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
MRI identifies edema and guides **muscle biopsy**; EMG supports a myopathic pattern
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

leprosy.name: Leprosy
leprosy.scope: Tuberculoid leprosy, lepromatous leprosy, hypopigmented anesthetic skin lesions, peripheral nerve enlargement, acid-fast bacilli on skin biopsy, dapsone, rifampin, clofazimine
leprosy.core: A hypopigmented or reddish patch with definite sensory loss and an enlarged peripheral nerve suggests Hansen disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prolonged close contact with untreated disease, residence in endemic regions; armadillo exposure in southern US
Mycobacterium leprae spreads mainly through respiratory droplets with sustained exposure; casual contact low risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Anesthetic skin lesions**: test light touch, pain and temperature
Thickened ulnar/common peroneal nerves, distal weakness, painless wounds; cool body areas preferentially involved
Lepromatous disease may cause diffuse infiltration, eyebrow loss, nasal involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organism infects macrophages and Schwann cells; cellular immunity determines disease spectrum
Strong Th1 response limits bacilli; weak cellular immunity permits widespread multibacillary infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Skin biopsy** with Fite acid-fast stain; slit-skin smear supports multibacillary disease
Histology: tuberculoid granulomas with few bacilli; lepromatous foamy macrophages with abundant organisms
Negative smear does not exclude paucibacillary disease; assess ocular, motor and sensory function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ WHO multidrug regimen: **rifampin + dapsone + clofazimine** for both categories
Paucibacillary: 6 months; multibacillary: 12 months; US regimens may differ—specialist coordination
Acute neuritis/reversal reaction → corticosteroids while continuing antimicrobials
Erythema nodosum leprosum: corticosteroids; severe refractory cases → thalidomide with strict pregnancy prevention
Dapsone: hemolysis/methemoglobinemia, especially G6PD deficiency; clofazimine: skin discoloration

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent neuropathy, claw hand, foot drop, resorption after repeated injury; corneal injury/blindness

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Early treatment and contact evaluation**; eligible contacts may receive single-dose rifampin prophylaxis
Daily skin/foot inspection, protective footwear, eye protection and rehabilitation prevent secondary disability

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vitiligo: depigmented skin with normal sensation
Tinea versicolor: fine scale, positive KOH, preserved sensation

table.title: Clinical poles
rows: Few sharply defined asymmetric patches; low burden
Numerous symmetric poorly defined lesions; high burden

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; CSF leak → pneumococcus; advanced HIV/transplant → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: CSF antigen/culture and opening pressure; TB studies for subacute low-glucose lymphocytic profile

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal close contacts → **rifampin or ceftriaxone** promptly; droplet isolation until 24 hours effective treatment
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, family history; EBV exposure, smoking and low vitamin D association

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular visual loss, impaired color vision, afferent pupillary defect
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse → **high-dose methylprednisolone**; severe steroid-refractory attack → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

muscular-dystrophies.name: Muscular dystrophies
muscular-dystrophies.scope: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin frameshift, Gowers sign, dilated cardiomyopathy), Becker muscular dystrophy, myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat, myotonia, cataracts, balding), genetic testing
muscular-dystrophies.core: Progressive inherited muscle weakness: childhood pelvic-girdle weakness suggests dystrophinopathy; delayed relaxation with multisystem disease suggests myotonic dystrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Duchenne/Becker: X-linked recessive; affected boys, maternal carrier relatives; de novo variants common
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant with anticipation; severe congenital disease often maternally transmitted

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gowers maneuver** and calf pseudohypertrophy indicate proximal weakness
Dystrophinopathy: waddling gait, delayed motor milestones; preserved sensation
Grip/percussion myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation, often improving with repeated movement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dystrophin deficiency destabilizes muscle membrane → myofiber necrosis and fat/fibrous replacement
Myotonic dystrophy: toxic expanded-repeat RNA disrupts splicing in multiple tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK → genetic testing**; dystrophin deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing if needed
Myotonic phenotype → DMPK repeat-expansion testing; muscle biopsy rarely needed
ECG/echocardiography and pulmonary function at diagnosis and serially; assess swallowing and sleep ventilation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Duchenne: **prednisone or deflazacort**, stretching, mobility support; specialist genotype-directed options
Cardiomyopathy → ACE inhibitor/ARB, add beta-blocker; respiratory weakness → assisted cough/noninvasive ventilation
Disabling myotonia → mexiletine after cardiac evaluation; high-grade conduction block → pacemaker
Avoid succinylcholine; dystrophinopathy also carries rhabdomyolysis risk with volatile anesthetics

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, restrictive respiratory failure, aspiration, scoliosis, contractures
Steroid-associated osteoporosis and adrenal suppression; myotonic dystrophy → sudden cardiac death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Carrier testing and genetic counseling**; screen female dystrophin carriers for cardiomyopathy
Vaccination, nutritional support, bone health monitoring, regular cardiac/respiratory surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: SMA: areflexia, fasciculations, relatively modest CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: acquired weakness, inflammation; no characteristic inheritance pattern

table.title: Distinguishing types
rows: Distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy

muscular-dystrophies.evidence: Not checked online; established phenotypes and supportive treatment; novel genotype-specific treatments omitted.

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea ethically permissible despite foreseeable unintended risks

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids** to symptoms; add stimulant laxative for constipation, reassess sedation/respiration

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Medicare hospice election concerns terminal-illness treatment; unrelated conditions remain treatable
No DNR requirement for hospice; enrollment can be revoked if goals change

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

parasomnias.name: Parasomnias
parasomnias.scope: REM sleep behavior disorder (polysomnography, clonazepam), sleep terrors, sleepwalking (somnambulism), nightmare disorder, isolated sleep paralysis, reassurance
parasomnias.core: Unusual behavior or experiences during sleep are classified by timing, recall, and whether REM muscle atonia is lost or persists.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sleep deprivation, stress, fever, alcohol, OSA precipitate NREM arousals
REM behavior disorder: older men, synucleinopathies, SSRIs; sleepwalking/terrors often childhood

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Dream enactment with injury** → ask bed partner about kicking, punching, falling from bed
Isolated sleep paralysis: conscious but briefly unable to move at sleep onset or awakening

rows.label: Pathophys
items: NREM disorders: incomplete arousal from deep sleep; REM behavior disorder: loss of normal skeletal atonia
Sleep paralysis: REM atonia persists into wakefulness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected REM behavior disorder → **video polysomnography** demonstrating REM without atonia
Typical childhood NREM events: clinical; atypical stereotyped episodes → video EEG/PSG
Assess snoring, sleep schedule, drugs, trauma, daytime sleep attacks

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ REM behavior disorder: **immediate-release melatonin or clonazepam**; melatonin favored with falls/OSA concerns
Sleep terrors/walking: reassurance, adequate sleep, scheduled awakenings for predictable frequent events
Nightmares: imagery rehearsal; trauma-associated nightmares → assess PTSD
Isolated paralysis: reassurance, regular sleep; accompanying cataplexy → evaluate narcolepsy

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury to sleeper/partner; clonazepam can worsen sedation, balance, sleep-disordered breathing
REM behavior disorder may precede Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, or multiple system atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Safe bedroom**: remove weapons, pad furniture, secure windows; separate sleeping if violent
Avoid sleep deprivation/alcohol; treat OSA; review triggering antidepressants

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nocturnal seizures: brief stereotyped clusters, possible postictal findings
OSA: gasping arousals tied to obstructive respiratory events

table.title: Timing and recall
rows: Awake, oriented, detailed frightening dream recall

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, physical/speech/swallow rehabilitation; selected refractory fluctuations/tremor → **deep brain stimulation**
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Essential tremor: action/postural tremor without decrementing bradykinesia
Drug-induced: blocker exposure, often symmetric; normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, urinary/cognitive symptoms

table.title: Atypical parkinsonism
rows: Severe orthostasis/urinary dysfunction, possible cerebellar signs
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle

rows.label: Dx
