items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; urgent Doppler exam in acute ischemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia → prompt limb-salvage evaluation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin and immediate vascular consultation**; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible limb may require primary amputation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings

table.title: Clinical stages
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals

peripheral-neuropathy.name: Peripheral neuropathy
peripheral-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, chemotherapy-induced (cisplatin, paclitaxel), HIV-associated neuropathy, alcohol-related, neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy (TCAs, gabapentinoids, SNRIs)
peripheral-neuropathy.core: Length-dependent injury produces symmetric distal sensory symptoms beginning in the feet and progressing proximally before the hands become involved.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, alcohol use, CKD, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, HIV
Cisplatin/paclitaxel exposure; older neurotoxic ART such as stavudine; malnutrition

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning pain, allodynia or numbness; reduced vibration, ankle reflexes and distal sensation
★ **Asymmetry, rapid progression, motor predominance or marked autonomic findings** → urgent expanded evaluation
Small-fiber neuropathy: pain/temperature loss with initially preserved strength and nerve conduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axonal dying-back affects longest fibers first; demyelinating neuropathy produces disproportionate conduction slowing

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose/A1c, B12 with methylmalonic acid if borderline, SPEP with immunofixation**
CBC, metabolic panel, TSH; HIV testing according to exposure and clinical context
EMG/nerve conduction for atypical features, unclear diagnosis, or suspected demyelination
Normal studies do not exclude small-fiber disease; skin biopsy can confirm selected cases

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat cause: glycemic control, B12, alcohol cessation/nutrition, optimize ART; review neurotoxic drugs
★ Pain → **duloxetine, gabapentin/pregabalin, or TCA**; choose by comorbidity and adverse effects
Gabapentinoids: sedation/edema, renal dose adjustment; TCAs: anticholinergic effects, cardiac risk in older adults
★ Painful chemotherapy neuropathy → **duloxetine**; discuss dose reduction/substitution with oncology
Topical lidocaine/capsaicin for localized symptoms; avoid chronic opioids

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, painless ulcers, infection, Charcot arthropathy; orthostatic hypotension with autonomic involvement
Pain treatment reduces symptoms without restoring lost sensation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Daily foot inspection, protective footwear, monofilament assessment, fall prevention
Treat nutritional deficiencies; monitor symptoms during neurotoxic chemotherapy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Radiculopathy: dermatomal, often asymmetric pain and weakness
Myelopathy: hyperreflexia, sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses rather than sensory stocking loss

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular activation/CGRP signaling; aura reflects cortical spreading depolarization
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent/disabling migraine → propranolol, topiramate, or CGRP-directed prevention; avoid topiramate/valproate in pregnancy
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

prion-disease.name: Prion disease
prion-disease.scope: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sporadic, familial, variant), rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus, ataxia, 14-3-3 protein, RT-QuIC, periodic sharp wave complexes, spongiform encephalopathy
prion-disease.core: Cognitive decline over weeks to months with stimulus-sensitive jerks and cerebellar dysfunction suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sporadic CJD usually older adults; familial cases involve autosomal dominant PRNP variants
Iatrogenic: contaminated neurosurgical equipment/tissue; variant CJD: bovine spongiform encephalopathy-contaminated beef

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Rapid progression** to akinetic mutism; visual, pyramidal, or extrapyramidal abnormalities
Startle myoclonus often develops after initial behavioral or memory changes
Variant CJD: younger age, early psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory complaints; prolonged course

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Misfolded protein templates conversion of normal prion protein; no nucleic acid
Neuronal loss, gliosis and vacuolation → spongiform encephalopathy without prominent inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Brain **MRI DWI**: cortical ribboning and caudate/putamen diffusion restriction
★ CSF **RT-QuIC** detects abnormal prion seeding; high specificity
CSF 14-3-3 reflects rapid neuronal injury; supportive but nonspecific
EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes; absence does not exclude disease
Exclude treatable mimics: CSF inflammatory/infectious studies, metabolic testing, autoimmune evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive/palliative care**; no established disease-modifying treatment
Clonazepam or levetiracetam for distressing myoclonus; nutrition and caregiver support
Brain biopsy rarely needed; notify infection control before invasive tissue procedures

rows.label: Complications
items: Dysphagia, aspiration, immobility; sporadic CJD usually fatal within one year

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prion-specific instrument decontamination or disposal; routine sterilization insufficient
Familial disease → genetic counseling; casual contact does not transmit CJD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autoimmune encephalitis: seizures, inflammatory findings; potentially immunotherapy-responsive
Alzheimer disease: progression over years
Wernicke encephalopathy: malnutrition, ophthalmoplegia; treat promptly with IV thiamine

prion-disease.evidence: Diagnosis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC CJD overview](https://www.cdc.gov/creutzfeldt-jakob/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); established supportive care.

restless-legs-syndrome.name: Restless legs syndrome
restless-legs-syndrome.scope: URGE criteria, iron deficiency association (ferritin <75), secondary causes (pregnancy, uremia, neuropathy), nonpharmacologic measures, iron replacement, dopamine agonists, alpha-2-delta ligands
restless-legs-syndrome.core: An uncomfortable urge to move the legs during rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening, disrupts sleep.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Iron deficiency, pregnancy, CKD/uremia, family history; neuropathy may coexist
Antihistamines, serotonergic antidepressants, dopamine antagonists, caffeine, alcohol and untreated OSA exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually bilateral deep crawling/aching sensations; neurologic examination often normal in primary disease
Repetitive sleep-related leg movements may coexist but are not required for diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Low brain iron and altered dopamine signaling; normal ferritin can mask functional iron deficiency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical URGE criteria**; symptoms not solely explained by cramps, posture or another disorder
★ Check **ferritin + transferrin saturation**, CBC and renal function; PSG usually unnecessary
Evaluate pregnancy, neuropathy and medications; isolated periodic limb movements alone ≠ RLS

rows.label: Tx
items: Regular sleep, moderate exercise, stretching/massage; remove exacerbating agents and treat OSA
★ **Iron replacement** if ferritin ≤75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation <20%
Oral ferrous sulfate when suitable; ferritin 75–100 or poor absorption/response → IV iron, often ferric carboxymaltose
★ Persistent symptoms → **gabapentin, pregabalin or gabapentin enacarbil**; adjust for renal function

rows.label: Complications
items: Insomnia, daytime fatigue, mood impairment; gabapentinoids cause sedation, edema and falls
Dopaminergic augmentation: earlier, stronger symptoms, spread to arms; impulse-control problems possible

rows.label: Prevention
items: Investigate and correct iron-loss source; repeat iron indices during replacement
Pregnancy: prioritize nonpharmacologic measures and iron; individualized obstetric medication review

rows.label: Mimics
items: Akathisia: generalized inner restlessness, medication-related, little circadian pattern
Nocturnal cramps: focal painful contraction, palpable muscle tightening
Neuropathy: persistent sensory symptoms not reliably relieved by movement

table.title: Dopaminergic drugs: AASM 2025
rows: Discouraged routinely; selected short-term use possible
Specialist gradual taper; avoid escalation or abrupt withdrawal

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

spinal-cord-injury.name: Spinal cord injury
spinal-cord-injury.scope: Traumatic spinal cord injury, incomplete cord syndromes, neurogenic shock, dermatome mapping, vertebral level
spinal-cord-injury.core: Trauma with weakness, a sensory level, and sphincter dysfunction demands spinal protection and urgent imaging; neurologic level may differ from vertebral injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Motor vehicle collision, falls, diving, penetrating injury; cervical stenosis predisposes to hyperextension injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute spinal shock: flaccid areflexia below lesion; later spasticity/hyperreflexia; assess sacral sparing
★ **Neurogenic shock**: hypotension, bradycardia, warm skin after high cord injury; exclude hemorrhage first
C3–5 involvement threatens diaphragmatic function; priapism and urinary retention support cord disruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Primary cord damage + secondary edema/ischemia; sympathetic interruption causes vasodilation and unopposed vagal tone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs with **cervical immobilization** → CT spine for fracture; persistent neurologic deficits → **MRI**
Document motor/sensory level, rectal tone, perianal sensation; S4–5 sparing defines incomplete injury
Dermatomes: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, S4–5 perianal
Motor: C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction
Cord ends around L1–2 vertebrae; lower vertebral injuries may damage nerve roots rather than cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Support ventilation, avoid hypoxia/hypotension; hemorrhage → blood; neurogenic shock → cautious fluids, **norepinephrine**
Urgent decompression/stabilization for compressive or unstable injuries; early specialist transfer
★ **No routine high-dose methylprednisolone**; infection/bleeding harms outweigh established benefit
Rehabilitation, pressure relief, intermittent catheterization, bowel regimen, VTE prophylaxis
Autonomic dysreflexia → sit upright, loosen clothing, empty bladder; persistent severe hypertension → topical nitroglycerin

rows.label: Complications
items: Autonomic dysreflexia after injury ≥T6: bladder/bowel trigger → severe hypertension, headache, sweating above lesion
Pressure injuries, DVT/PE, recurrent UTI, respiratory failure, contractures, chronic neuropathic pain

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention, safe diving; maintain skin checks and bladder/bowel schedules

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cauda equina: asymmetric radicular pain, saddle anesthesia, LMN weakness, reduced reflexes
Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexia without discrete sensory level; often preceding infection

table.title: Incomplete cord syndromes
rows: Ipsilateral motor/vibration; contralateral pain/temperature starts 1–2 levels below

spinal-cord-injury.evidence: Autonomic dysreflexia checked 2026-10-30: [PVA clinician guideline](https://pva.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/cpg_autonomic-dysreflexia.pdf); remaining acute management: established trauma teaching.

subarachnoid-hemorrhage.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.scope: Ruptured saccular aneurysm, thunderclap headache, noncontrast head CT, lumbar puncture and xanthochromia, nimodipine, complications
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.core: Sudden headache maximal within seconds, often during exertion, with possible meningismus or collapse: presume subarachnoid hemorrhage until excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, hypertension, family history, prior aneurysm; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Ruptured saccular aneurysm usually near circle-of-Willis branch points; cocaine increases rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness, transient loss of consciousness; sentinel headache may precede major hemorrhage
★ **Painful pupil-involving CN III palsy** → posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Declining consciousness, focal deficits or seizures → high-risk presentation; normal examination does not exclude hemorrhage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Blood enters subarachnoid space → meningeal irritation, ↑ICP, impaired CSF resorption
Blood-breakdown products and vascular injury contribute to delayed cerebral ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT immediately**; sensitivity declines with elapsed time
★ Negative CT >6 hours after onset or neurologic deficit → **LP**, assessing xanthochromia and RBCs
High-quality CT within 6 hours, neurologically intact, expert interpretation → may exclude SAH without routine LP
Confirmed blood → **CT angiography**; negative/inconclusive CTA with suspected aneurysm → catheter angiography
Traumatic tap may show falling RBCs; clearing alone cannot reliably exclude SAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Support airway, reverse anticoagulation, analgesia; severe hypertension → IV nicardipine; avoid hypotension/BP swings
★ **Urgent aneurysm coiling or clipping**, preferably within 24 hours, prevents rebleeding
★ **Enteral nimodipine for 21 days**, maintain euvolemia; no prophylactic hypervolemia
Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus → external ventricular drainage
Secured aneurysm + delayed ischemia → induced hypertension; refractory → endovascular vasodilator/angioplasty

rows.label: Complications
items: Early rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizures; delayed ischemia typically days 3–14
Hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; stress cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation and BP control; specialist screening discussion for ≥2 affected first-degree relatives or high-risk ADPKD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction: recurrent thunderclap headaches; segmental angiographic narrowing
Meningitis: fever and inflammatory CSF rather than aneurysmal bleeding
Migraine: usually slower onset, recurrent stereotyped episodes; first thunderclap still needs hemorrhage evaluation

syncope.name: Syncope
syncope.scope: Vasovagal / neurocardiogenic syncope, orthostatic syncope, situational syncope, cardiogenic syncope, breath-holding spells, cerebral hypoperfusion workup
syncope.core: Brief loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid spontaneous recovery; identify cardiac danger before labeling an episode reflex-mediated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dehydration, blood loss, autonomic dysfunction, diuretics/vasodilators; prolonged standing, heat, fear
Structural heart disease, conduction disease, arrhythmias, family history of sudden death

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Exertional or supine syncope**, palpitations, absent prodrome, cardiac murmur → high-risk cause
Reflex prodrome: nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, tunnel vision; may include brief myoclonic jerks
Situational triggers: urination, coughing, defecation; breath-holding spells follow crying/pain in young children

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Vasodilation/bradycardia, failed postural compensation, or low cardiac output transiently limits cerebral flow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Initial **history, examination, orthostatic BP, ECG**; bedside glucose and targeted pregnancy/bleeding evaluation
Orthostasis: systolic fall ≥20 or diastolic ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes standing
High-risk → admission/monitoring; suspected structural disease → echo; intermittent arrhythmia → ambulatory ECG
Tilt-table testing for recurrent unexplained reflex/orthostatic cases; no routine head CT, EEG, carotid ultrasound
Typical breath-holding spells: normal development, awake trigger, rapid recovery; CBC/ferritin and ECG when evaluating

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reflex event → supine, legs elevated; **hydration, counterpressure maneuvers**, trigger recognition
Orthostatic cause → replace volume, review drugs, rise slowly, compression; refractory neurogenic cases → midodrine
★ Cardiac cause → **treat rhythm/obstruction**, restrict unsafe activity pending evaluation
Breath-holding: reassure caregivers, safe positioning, treat iron deficiency; no antiseizure drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, fractures, driving injury; underlying cardiac disease carries sudden-death risk
Recurrent episodes → activity limitation, anxiety; pressor drugs can cause supine hypertension

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid dehydration and prolonged immobility; individualized driving/activity restrictions after unexplained or cardiac events

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seizure: prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue biting
Hypoglycemia: persistent altered state until glucose corrected
TIA: focal deficit; isolated transient unconsciousness unusual

syncope.evidence: Not checked online; established syncope evaluation teaching.

traumatic-brain-injury.name: Traumatic brain injury
traumatic-brain-injury.scope: Epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, cerebral contusion, diffuse axonal injury, concussion, elevated ICP
traumatic-brain-injury.core: Head trauma ranges from transient functional disturbance to expanding hemorrhage; serial neurologic deterioration requires urgent imaging and neurosurgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Falls, crashes, assault, sports; anticoagulation increases bleeding
Older age, alcohol use and cerebral atrophy predispose to bridging-vein injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, vomiting, amnesia; focal deficit or progressive somnolence suggests structural injury
★ **Unilateral fixed dilated pupil + declining consciousness** → uncal herniation
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; late sign of critically elevated ICP

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impact/shear → secondary edema, ischemia, excitotoxicity
Rising intracranial volume → reduced cerebral perfusion; hypotension/hypoxia sharply worsen secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs/cervical protection → **GCS, pupils, focal examination**, repeated serially
**Noncontrast head CT** for moderate/severe injury or mild injury with high-risk features
High-risk features: anticoagulation, skull-fracture signs, focal deficit, repeated vomiting, worsening symptoms
GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤8 severe; diffuse axonal injury may require MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **GCS ≤8 → intubate** with spinal protection; prevent hypoxemia/hypotension; reverse anticoagulants promptly
Expanding hematoma, mass effect or deterioration → urgent neurosurgical evacuation; observation only with close monitoring
★ Elevated ICP → head elevation, analgesia/sedation, **hypertonic saline or mannitol**; treat sustained ICP >22 mm Hg
Herniation → brief hyperventilation as bridge; avoid routine prophylactic hyperventilation and corticosteroids
Severe/high-risk TBI → levetiracetam for 7 days; refractory ICP → neurosurgical decompression

rows.label: Complications
items: Posttraumatic seizures, chronic cognitive/behavioral impairment, postconcussion syndrome, hydrocephalus
Skull-base fracture → CSF leak/meningitis; avoid nasal instrumentation with suspected basilar fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid alcohol-related injury
Concussion: no same-day sports; relative rest 24–48 hours → graded recovery/clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Intoxication: may coexist; exclude intracranial injury before attributing depressed consciousness to substances

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.scope: Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, oculomotor dysfunction), Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, amnesia), thiamine (B1) deficiency, IV thiamine before glucose, mammillary body atrophy
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.core: Malnourished adult with confusion, gait ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; the complete Wernicke triad is often absent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, starvation, inadequate parenteral nutrition
Carbohydrate loading or refeeding increases thiamine demand in depleted patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Hypothermia, hypotension, or coma signal severe deficiency
★ Korsakoff: disproportionate **anterograde amnesia**, retrograde memory loss, confabulation; relatively preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate metabolism → ATP failure and selective neuronal injury
Medial thalami, periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies injured → persistent amnestic syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; do not wait for vitamin assays or imaging before treatment
MRI may show symmetric thalamic/periaqueductal lesions; normal MRI does not exclude Wernicke
Chronic disease: mammillary body atrophy; evaluate glucose, electrolytes, magnesium, and competing encephalopathy causes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke → **high-dose IV thiamine**, followed by oral replacement after stabilization
Give thiamine before or with glucose when feasible; never delay emergency dextrose for hypoglycemia
Replete magnesium, fluid/electrolyte deficits; restore nutrition cautiously and treat alcohol withdrawal separately
Ocular findings may improve rapidly; gait/cognition recover more slowly; established amnesia often persists

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated encephalopathy → death or irreversible Korsakoff syndrome; falls and impaired independent living
Refeeding syndrome → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmias, respiratory weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Routine oral **thiamine supplementation** for persistent malnutrition; nutritional assessment during alcohol treatment
Alcohol cessation support, balanced nutrition; monitor intake after bariatric surgery or prolonged vomiting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, hallucinations after reduced intake
Hepatic encephalopathy: cirrhosis, asterixis, precipitating bleed or infection
Posterior circulation stroke: abrupt focal deficits; diffusion MRI identifies infarction
